title: Chapter XVII

teacherSummary.text: The creature demands a female companion as wretched as himself, promising to withdraw to South America. Moved and afraid, Victor agrees.

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track; this novel is above the grades 6–8 complexity band, so work from the passage your teacher selects). In “Chapter XVII,” how does Shelley show the demand for a companion? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the passage, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the theme you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Chapter XVII, how does Shelley develop the idea of the demand for a companion? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the theme in the chapter helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter XVII develops the idea of the demand for a companion. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of theme and characterization shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Chapter XVII (where it begins, turns and ends) and its theme shape the reader's understanding of the demand for a companion. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Chapter XVII suggests about the demand for a companion. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the chapter's theme and characterization), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Mary Shelley uses theme in Chapter XVII to complicate the reader's understanding of the demand for a companion. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter XVII within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of the demand for a companion responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Chapter XVII alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the chapter's handling of the demand for a companion follows or bends those conventions, using the theme as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Chapter XVII and its treatment of the demand for a companion. State your method, show what it reveals in the chapter's theme and characterization, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Chapter XVII as evidence for a larger claim about the demand for a companion in Frankenstein. Connect close reading of the chapter to the whole novel, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter XVII as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of the demand for a companion. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Frankenstein.

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: Is the creature's request fair? What risks does Victor consider? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are insurmountable, concede, trifled, protectors, sickened. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check the definition. Here is the first: “But that cannot be; the human senses are insurmountable barriers to our union.” In this sentence it means: impossible to overcome. Word histories: For the other words, look up the word history (Etymonline or the OED) and record the language of origin and the root meaning in your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Frankenstein would have known. Debates on whether humans have natural rights to companionship and happiness echo Enlightenment philosophy. Why does this chapter matter? This bargain is the hinge of the plot; Victor's later choice will decide everyone's fate. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for theme.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. The passage opens: ““You must create a female for me, with whom I can live in the interchange of those sympathies necessary for my being.” I stop and ask: what is the author doing here, and how does it connect to the demand for a companion? I circle “concede”, one of today's words, and ask why the author chose it over a plainer word. When I find theme, I underline it and write its effect in the margin, then I check my idea against the next sentence.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for theme.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of theme. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.
segments.passage: “You must create a female for me, with whom I can live in the interchange of those sympathies necessary for my being. This you alone can do; and I demand it of you as a right which you must not refuse to concede.”

segments.activity: Students annotate a new passage independently in the reader, then begin the writing prompt at their assigned rigor level.
segments.script: Your turn. Annotate the next page in the app for Theme, Characterization, Conflict: at least three marks with a margin note each. Then open your writing prompt; the app shows the level your teacher assigned (for a 9–10 class, the HS Sophomore prompt reads: Analyze how Chapter XVII develops the idea of the demand for a companion. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of theme and characterization shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.) I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion (think-pair-share or a short Socratic circle).
segments.script: Let's talk. Our question: How does this chapter connect to the costs of unchecked ambition? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence.

segments.activity: Chapter quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the chapter quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this chapter suggests about the demand for a companion, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Today we saw how theme shapes the demand for a companion. Tonight, read the next chapter and add two words to your etymology log.
